presidents.name: George Washington
presidents.summary: Washington enslaved people for his entire adult life and continued to do so throughout his presidency, moving enslaved household workers between Virginia and Philadelphia to keep Pennsylvania's gradual abolition law from freeing them. As president he signed the Fugitive Slave Act of 1793, and his will directed that the 123 people he owned outright be freed after his wife's death.
presidents.paragraph: Washington took office already holding people in bondage, and he kept doing it in the president's houses in New York and Philadelphia. At least ten enslaved people worked in those households, including Ona Judge, Hercules and William Lee, and when Attorney General Edmund Randolph warned the Washingtons that Pennsylvania's 1780 gradual abolition law freed anyone who lived in the state six straight months, the family rotated enslaved workers back to Mount Vernon to reset the clock. In February 1793 Washington signed the Fugitive Slave Act, which let enslavers pursue and reclaim people who had escaped into free states. He also signed the 1789 act continuing the Northwest Ordinance, which barred slavery north of the Ohio, and the 1794 act banning American ships from carrying slaves to foreign ports. When Ona Judge escaped in May 1796, Washington used federal officials to try to get her back, and tried again in 1799. His will freed the 123 people he owned outright, but only after Martha's death.

callouts.text: Washington signed "An Act respecting fugitives from justice, and persons escaping from the service of their masters" on February 12, 1793, creating a federal process for reclaiming people who escaped slavery across state lines.

presidents.personalRecord: Washington enslaved people from adolescence until his death on December 14, 1799. A list he compiled in June 1799 enumerated 317 people at Mount Vernon: those he owned outright, the Custis "dower" people he controlled through Martha but could not legally free, and others leased from a neighbor. Encyclopedia Virginia states his will "decreed that all 123 of his enslaved people be freed upon the death of his wife," with those under twenty-five to be taught to read and write; the Miller Center describes the will as freeing one man outright and manumitting "roughly over a hundred" others. He could not free the Custis dower people, and they were dispersed to Custis heirs.

presidents.name: John Adams
presidents.summary: Adams did not own enslaved people and staffed his official households with paid white and free Black workers, though the White House Historical Association notes the Adamses may at times have hired enslaved workers from their owners. In foreign policy his administration broke with the pattern of the era by aiding Toussaint Louverture in Saint-Domingue against his British-backed rivals.
presidents.paragraph: Adams is one of the few early presidents who never enslaved anyone. When he and Abigail set up official households in New York, Philadelphia and then Washington, they hired white and free African American servants instead of bringing enslaved workers the way Washington and the Virginians did. That doesn't mean they stood outside the system: the White House Historical Association says they tolerated slavery in daily life and may have hired enslaved African Americans from their owners, paying the wages to the owners. Adams had also taken cases in Massachusetts in which, as he later put it, "Negroes sued for their Freedom." The sharpest break came abroad. Where the previous administration had worried about a Black-led revolution in the Caribbean, Adams decided to send aid to Toussaint Louverture against his British-supported rivals, partly on antislavery grounds and partly to keep the trade of Saint-Domingue open during the Quasi-War with France.

callouts.text: Adams was the first president who owned no enslaved people, hiring white and free African American workers for the vice president's and president's houses between 1789 and 1801.

presidents.personalRecord: Adams never owned enslaved people. The White House Historical Association states flatly that "Adams did not own enslaved people" and that the family hired white and free African American workers instead, while noting the possibility that enslaved people were hired from their owners for household work. Because he held no one in bondage, there is no manumission or estate distribution to record at his death in 1826.

presidents.name: Thomas Jefferson
presidents.summary: Jefferson enslaved more than 600 people over his lifetime and continued to do so throughout his presidency and until his death. As president he called on Congress to end American participation in the transatlantic slave trade and signed the 1807 act prohibiting it, while also signing the 1806 law cutting off trade with Haiti and refusing to recognize Haitian independence.
presidents.paragraph: Jefferson wrote about slavery as an evil and kept practicing it. Encyclopedia Virginia says he owned more than 600 people over his life and freed only a handful, and in Notes on the State of Virginia he advanced the claim that Black people were limited in intellect and imagination. In December 1806 he told Congress the time had come to withdraw Americans from "those violations of human rights" committed on the inhabitants of Africa, and on March 2, 1807 he signed the act barring the importation of enslaved people after January 1, 1808. That same term he moved the other direction on Haiti: in February 1806 he signed a law prohibiting commercial intercourse with the parts of Saint-Domingue not under French control, and his government cut off aid to Toussaint Louverture and withheld recognition, which the United States would not extend until 1862.

callouts.text: In his annual message of December 2, 1806, Jefferson urged Congress to use its new constitutional authority to withdraw Americans from the African slave trade at the earliest date allowed.

presidents.personalRecord: Encyclopedia Virginia states Jefferson "owned more than 600 enslaved persons at one time or another, of which he freed only a handful." He enslaved people throughout his presidency and until his death on July 4, 1826. His will and codicil freed five members of the Hemings family, including the men Burwell Colbert, John Hemmings and Joseph Fossett, and Madison and Eston Hemings, whom Encyclopedia Virginia describes as likely his sons by Sally Hemings. Sally Hemings herself was not freed by the will; ownership passed to his daughter Martha Jefferson Randolph. Most of the people he enslaved were sold after his death to cover his debts.

presidents.name: James Madison
presidents.summary: Madison enslaved more than 100 people at Montpelier and brought enslaved workers from the plantation into the White House, including Paul Jennings, who came to Washington at age ten. He freed no one at his death in 1836, and later pinned his hopes for ending slavery on compensated emancipation combined with removing free Black people from the country.
presidents.paragraph: Madison lived his whole adult life on labor he did not pay for. Historians have identified 300 people enslaved at Montpelier, with more than 100 there at any one time, and Encyclopedia Virginia says Madison "enslaved more than 100 people" and did not emancipate them despite his stated misgivings. Enslaved workers came with him to Washington: Paul Jennings, born at Montpelier in 1799, accompanied the Madisons to the capital at age ten and served as a footman in the presidential household, later writing the first memoir of life in the White House. Madison's answer to slavery was removal. He hoped for compensated emancipation tied to relocating freed people abroad, possibly in Liberia, and in 1833 he became president of the American Colonization Society. He freed no one at his death. Dolley Madison later sold Jennings for $200; Daniel Webster then bought him for $120 and let him buy himself out at $8 a month.

presidents.personalRecord: Madison enslaved people from inheritance until his death on June 28, 1836. Encyclopedia Virginia says he "enslaved more than 100 people" and "did not emancipate his own enslaved workers," and the Miller Center records that he "emancipated only one enslaved person, Billey" and bequeathed the rest to his wife. Historians have identified 300 people enslaved at Montpelier across its history. In 1834, two years before his death, Madison sold sixteen enslaved people to a relative in Louisiana to pay debts. Dolley Madison still owned roughly seventy-five people when Montpelier was sold in 1844.

presidents.name: James Monroe
presidents.summary: Monroe enslaved 178 people over his adult life and freed one, Peter Marks, in his final days. As president he signed the Missouri Compromise on March 6, 1820, admitting Missouri as a slave state while barring slavery north of 36°30' in the rest of the Louisiana Purchase, and signed the 1819 slave trade act under which the settlement that became Liberia was established, its capital named Monrovia for him.
presidents.paragraph: Monroe had already dealt with Black resistance up close before he was president. As governor of Virginia in 1800 he handled Gabriel's Conspiracy, an insurrection plot by an enslaved blacksmith; twenty-six men were hanged, and Monroe wrote to Jefferson asking how many executions would be enough to deter another rising. In the White House he signed the two laws that framed federal slavery policy for a generation. The act of March 3, 1819 authorized the Navy to seize slave ships and to place recaptured Africans with agents on the African coast, the mechanism that produced the Liberia settlement whose capital was named Monrovia after him. Then on March 6, 1820 he signed the Missouri Compromise, which admitted Missouri and forever prohibited slavery in Louisiana Purchase territory north of 36°30' — with a clause letting enslavers reclaim anyone who escaped into that free territory. He enslaved people the entire time.

callouts.text: Monroe signed the Missouri Compromise on March 6, 1820, prohibiting slavery in Louisiana Purchase territory north of 36°30' north latitude while admitting Missouri as a state, with a clause preserving enslavers' right to reclaim escapees there.

presidents.personalRecord: Monroe's Highland (owned by William & Mary) documents "178 individuals who led their lives—in part or wholly—enslaved by Monroe during his adulthood," including 53 people at Highland under his ownership. He freed one person: "Peter Marks, who was manumitted in a request Monroe made during the last days of his life." When Monroe sold Highland's farmland in 1828, many of the people he enslaved were sold south to Florida, with Monroe directing the buyer, Colonel Joseph White, to keep existing families together.

presidents.name: John Quincy Adams
presidents.summary: Adams never owned enslaved people, but the White House Historical Association documents enslaved workers living in his White House through his wife's Maryland relatives, including a man named Holzey whose death Adams recorded in his diary in February 1828. His sustained public record against slavery came after the presidency, in nine terms in the House fighting the gag rule and in his 1841 Supreme Court argument in the Amistad case.
presidents.paragraph: Adams's presidency is not where his antislavery reputation was made. He owned no one, and the White House Historical Association notes that he and his father were the only two of the first seven presidents who did not bring enslaved people into the White House. But the same research finds that enslaved workers attached to his wife's Hellen relatives lived under his roof. On February 23, 1828 Adams wrote in his diary that "Holzey, the black boy belonging to Johnson Hellen, and who has been several years with us," had died; two days later, on the day of her wedding in the White House, Mary Catherine Hellen filed manumission papers for an enslaved woman named Rachel Clark. Adams later said he abhorred slavery and did not suffer it in his family. What he did afterward is the sharper record: elected to the House in 1830, he spent eight years fighting the gag rule that tabled antislavery petitions without debate, and in 1841 he argued the Amistad case before the Supreme Court and won the Africans' freedom.

presidents.personalRecord: Adams never owned enslaved people; the Miller Center lists him as "one of the only US presidents not to own slaves," and the White House Historical Association says he and his father were the only two of the first seven presidents who did not bring enslaved people into the White House. He himself claimed in 1832 that he "abhorred slavery [and] did not suffer it in my family." The same research finds substantial evidence that enslaved people attached to his wife's Hellen relatives lived in his household, including in the White House, and that his 1820 census entry listed one enslaved girl under fourteen. There is no manumission by him to record, because he owned no one.

disputes: Whether Adams's household used enslaved labor: the conventional account (and Adams's own 1832 statement) says he never suffered slavery in his family, while the White House Historical Association's research finds considerable evidence that enslaved people belonging to his wife's relatives lived and worked in his home, including at the White House. Both are recorded.
